source_cards.front: What is the single most effective way to protect yourself in a crash?
source_cards.back: Wearing a seat belt correctly is the single most effective way to protect yourself and sharply cuts your risk of a fatal injury in a crash.

source_cards.front: Where should the shoulder belt and the lap belt sit?
source_cards.back: The shoulder belt goes snugly across the middle of the chest and shoulder, never behind your back, under your arm, or across the neck or face, and the lap belt holds the hips snugly below the stomach.

source_cards.front: Who in a moving vehicle must be belted or restrained?
source_cards.back: Under RCW forty-six point six one.six hundred eighty-seven and RCW forty-six point six one.six hundred eighty-eight, all occupants of a moving vehicle need a fastened seat belt or an approved child restraint, and driving or riding without one is illegal.

source_cards.front: Which three separate fit checks involve the headrest and belt?
source_cards.back: The headrest lines up with your ears, while the lap belt rests on the upper thighs and the cross strap on mid-shoulder, three separate fit checks.

source_cards.front: What standards must child restraints meet, and who can check the installation?
source_cards.back: Child restraints must meet Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards and be installed following both the vehicle and the seat maker's instructions, and a certified child passenger safety technician can check the installation.

source_cards.front: How long should a child stay in each restraint stage, and how do children ride until age two?
source_cards.back: Keep a child in each restraint stage as long as that seat allows, and a child from birth until age two must use a car seat that faces the rear.

source_cards.front: How must children aged two to four ride?
source_cards.back: Children aged two to four must ride in a car seat with a harness, which may face either rearward or forward.

source_cards.front: How long do children aged four and older stay in a car or booster seat?
source_cards.back: Children aged four and older stay in a car or booster seat until the vehicle's lap and shoulder belts fit properly, usually between ages eight and twelve, and the booster stage covers kids from four years old up to a height of four feet nine inches.

source_cards.front: Who must wear a properly fitting seat belt instead of a booster?
source_cards.back: Anyone taller than four feet nine inches who is old enough for a seat belt must wear a properly fitting belt.

source_cards.front: Why must you be belted when airbags deploy, and who should never ride in front?
source_cards.back: Airbags work together with seat belts, so an unbelted occupant risks serious injury or death when an airbag deploys, and children under thirteen should never ride in the front seat.

source_cards.front: At what age do the harness stage and the booster stage meet?
source_cards.back: Children aged two to four ride in a harnessed car seat, while from age four they move to a car or booster seat until the adult belt fits, so the harness stage and the booster stage meet at age four.

source_cards.front: Where do pedestrians have the right-of-way?
source_cards.back: Always yield to pedestrians, who, like bicyclists, hold the right-of-way at every crosswalk and intersection, marked or unmarked.

source_cards.front: What rights and duties do bicyclists have, and why are they at high risk?
source_cards.back: Bicyclists carry the same rights and duties as vehicle drivers, and because bikes are small and hard to see, riders face a high risk of serious injury or death.

source_cards.front: May a bicyclist use the full lane, and how much space do you leave when following?
source_cards.back: A bicyclist may legally use the full lane, you may not share a lane with one, and when following a bicyclist you leave at least three feet of space.

source_cards.front: How is a bicyclist riding in a crosswalk treated?
source_cards.back: A bicyclist riding in a crosswalk counts as a pedestrian, so you must yield in marked and unmarked crosswalks alike.

source_cards.front: How is a bicyclist treated on the road versus in a crosswalk?
source_cards.back: A bicyclist on the road is treated as a vehicle with a right to the full lane, but a bicyclist in a crosswalk is treated as a pedestrian you must yield to.

source_cards.front: How do you pass a bicyclist safely?
source_cards.back: To pass a bicyclist, move over a full lane when two lanes run your way, or use the other lane only without oncoming traffic, pass slowly on their left with at least three feet from your widest point, and do not pass just before a right turn.

source_cards.front: How is the passing gap for a bicyclist measured?
source_cards.back: The three-foot passing gap for a bicyclist is measured from the widest part of your vehicle, and with one lane each way you use the other lane only when no traffic is coming.

source_cards.front: What do bike lanes look like, and when may you drive in one?
source_cards.back: Bike lanes are often green with solid white lines and a bicycle symbol, and you may drive in one only to turn or to cross it to park at the curb.

source_cards.front: At a two-way stop, who has the right-of-way?

source_cards.front: How do turning yields differ at four-way and two-way stops?
source_cards.back: A left-turning driver yields to straight and right-turning traffic at a four-way stop, while at a two-way stop any turning driver yields to the one going straight.

source_cards.front: Why check behind for bicyclists before turning?

source_cards.front: What is a cross intersection?

source_cards.front: What is a T-intersection, and who has the right-of-way?
source_cards.back: A T-intersection is a three-way junction where one road ends at a through road, and a yield or stop sign there shows that through traffic has the right-of-way.

source_cards.front: At a Y-intersection, who has the right-of-way?
source_cards.back: At a Y-intersection a minor road joins a major route, often with a stop sign on the minor road, and cars on the major road have the right-of-way.

source_cards.front: Who waits at T and Y intersections?
source_cards.back: At a T-intersection the through road has priority, and at a Y-intersection the major road has priority, so in both the driver on the ending or minor road waits.

source_cards.front: What do you do entering and inside a roundabout?

source_cards.front: What do you do if an emergency vehicle approaches in a roundabout?

source_cards.front: What is a diverging diamond interchange?
source_cards.back: A diverging diamond is a newer Washington interchange that shifts traffic to the opposite side of the road so left turns onto and off freeway ramps flow better, with fewer crossing points and less crash risk.

source_cards.front: What causes a skid, and what is the best defense?
source_cards.back: A skid happens when tires lose their grip, made more likely by high speed and slick roads when you turn or stop suddenly, and the best defense is avoiding one.

source_cards.front: What do you do with your feet in a skid?
source_cards.back: In a skid, first lift your foot off the accelerator, then press or pump the brakes; without antilock brakes, stomping the pedal can worsen the skid.

source_cards.front: How does braking in a skid differ with and without antilock brakes?
source_cards.back: Antilock brakes let you keep steering while braking in a skid, whereas without them a quick hard press on the pedal can deepen the skid.

source_cards.front: Which way do you steer in a skid?
source_cards.back: During a skid, steer the way the vehicle is moving and keep correcting until the tires regain traction in the direction you steer.

source_cards.front: What is hydroplaning, and how do you prevent it?
source_cards.back: Hydroplaning is water building up between tires and road so they lose traction, and slowing down on wet roads is the best prevention.

source_cards.front: What do you do if you hydroplane?
source_cards.back: If you hydroplane, lift off the accelerator, brake gently, hold the wheel steady without jerking it, and look where you want to go.

source_cards.front: How does steering in a skid differ from steering while hydroplaning?
source_cards.back: In a skid you steer in the direction the car is moving and keep correcting, but when hydroplaning you hold the wheel steady and avoid any jerk or overcorrection.

source_cards.front: Why brake gently when hydroplaning?
source_cards.back: Without antilock brakes, pressing the pedal hard while hydroplaning can make it worse, which is why the guide says to brake gently.
